voice: Valory B – Conversational Girl-Next-Door with Relatable Vibe

lines.text: Here's what we're going to draw. Five rows, and the stars step in and back out again.
Easy enough to look at. The whole question is how you'd tell a computer to make it.
And before we draw a single star, there are two things we have to get straight. Skip them and everything after is magic — and magic's no use to you.
Five rows. To talk about them at all, we need a way of saying which one we mean.
So we number them going down. And here's the bit that catches everybody out — we start at nought, not one.
Nought. One. Two. Three. Four.
Five rows, and the last one is called four. That number is the row's name. It's called the index, and rows run up and down.
Now the same thing sideways, because I've been quietly using it and I haven't told you.
Every row is five squares across, and those get numbered too. Nought to four, left to right. Those are the columns.
So rows go up and down, columns go left and right. And that means every single square on this board has two names, not one.
This one is row two, column nought. That pair is the square's address — give me a row and a column and I can find any square there is.
And this one is row four, column three. Two names, always in that order: row first, then column.
Right. Now back to the rows, because that's where the pattern lives. Let's lay them out in a line so we can count along them.
Which one's in the middle? Come in one from the left, and one from the right. You land on row two.
Two above it, two below it. Row two is the middle, and it stays the middle for the rest of the lesson.
And now the only sum in this whole lesson. How many steps is a row from the middle? We're going to count them, one hop at a time.
Start on row nought. Hop across to row one. That's one step.
Hop again, onto row two. That's two — and we've arrived. So row nought is two steps from the middle.
Row one. One hop and you're there. One step.
And row two? Row two is the middle. You're already standing on it, so you don't move at all. Nought steps.
Row three. One hop back up. One step.
And row four. Two hops. Two steps.
Write them down in the order we found them. Two, one, nought, one, two. That's every number this lesson needs, and you counted all five yourself.
So what's it for? Here it is. That count tells you how many columns to leave empty at the start of the row, before the first star goes down.
Row nought counted two. So columns nought and one stay empty — those two, there.
And the star lands on column two. One star, and the row is done.
Row one counted one. Only column nought is empty, so the stars run from column one across to column three. Three of them.
Row two counted nought. Nothing is left empty at all. Stars from column nought right across to column four. Five.
Row three counted one again, the same as row one. So it gets the same row of stars back.
And row four counted two, like row nought. Two columns empty, one star. There's your diamond.
Look at the pairs. Row nought and row four match. Row one and row three match. That's not luck — they're the same distance from the middle, so they get the same row.
So the rule, in words: the empty columns are how far you are from the middle, and the stars are whatever's left once you've taken those off both ends.
Right. Now we write it down. Not all at once though — one line at a time, and you'll see every single one is something you already did by hand.
First line. We're just telling it how big this thing is. Five. Everything else works off that one number, so if you ever want a bigger diamond, this is the only line you'd touch.
Second line walks down the rows. That i is the row you're standing on — the index, the name we gave each row at the start.
The three bits in its brackets read in the order you'd say them out loud. Start at nought. Keep going while i is under five. Add one each time round.

Third line is your counting, squeezed into one line. n divided by two is two, the middle row. Take away the row you're on, and abs throws the minus sign away — you only ever cared how far, not which side.
Next two lines walk the empty columns. c is the column now, not the row — it starts at nought and stops when it reaches the gap. On row nought that's columns nought and one.
And that's the same for we just met, doing a smaller job. Repeating something a set number of times is the only thing a for loop ever does. Once you know it, you know it everywhere.

Then the stars, and read this one carefully — it carries on from where the spaces stopped. It starts at the gap and runs until five minus the gap. On row nought, that's column two, and then it's done.
This one just means the row is finished. Drop the pen to the next line down. It's pressing Enter, nothing more.
And the closing bracket says where the repeating stops. Everything inside it happens once per row — so five times over.
That's the lot. Nine lines, and there isn't one in there you didn't work out by hand first.
So now watch it go. I'll stop talking — this bit you just watch.
That's every square accounted for, one at a time, and the whole diamond out the other end.
And here's your reward for sitting through all that counting. Change one question — from how far from the middle, to how far from the nearest edge…
…and the very same program draws an hourglass instead. Same rows, same columns, same counting. One different question.
That's usually what separates two shapes. Not the code. The question.
